title: Pharmacology principles: how drugs move and act
note: Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to a drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME). Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body, usually by binding a receptor as an agonist or antagonist. Half-life, bioavailability and therapeutic index turn these ideas into numbers.

read.title: Half-life and steady state
text: Most drugs leave the body by first-order kinetics: in each unit of time, a constant fraction of the drug is removed, not a constant amount. The half-life is the time it takes for the plasma concentration to fall by half. After one half-life 50 percent remains, after two 25 percent, after three 12.5 percent. After four to five half-lives only about 3 to 6 percent is left, and the drug is usually considered effectively gone.

The same arithmetic governs how levels build up. When a drug is given repeatedly at a steady rate, the amount eliminated per hour rises as the concentration rises, until elimination matches intake. That balance point is steady state, and it is reached after about four to five half-lives. A drug with a 6-hour half-life reaches steady state in about a day; one with a 1-week half-life takes about a month or longer, which is why a loading dose is sometimes given to reach the target level sooner.

Half-life depends on two things: how widely a drug distributes (volume of distribution) and how efficiently the body clears it (clearance). A larger volume or slower clearance means a longer half-life.
